newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rexrodt takes new swipe at Waigel in budget row.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt takes new swipe at Waigel in budget row.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt renewed criticism of Finance Minister Theo Waigel in a row over economic forecasts on Monday, saying Waigel had been wrong to blame his department for skewing projections.

Waigel, in an interview with news weekly Der Spiegel, said other government departments had botched economic forecasts and left him searching for billions of marks to cut Bonn's deficit to meet the convergence criteria for European monetary union.
But Rexrodt, in Paris for OECD ministerial talks, said responsibility for the forecasts was shared widely.

"The economic estimates are the result of common work of the different ministries and not only of the economics ministry," Rexrodt told reporters on his arrival at the Paris headquarters of the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development.
"Therefore I have to reject his declaration that it would be our fault that the estimates were wrong," he said.
Rexrodt was due to represent Germany for the two-day annual OECD talks, which started on Monday, alongside Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.

Government feuding has broken out into the open after Waigel refused to rule out tax hikes to cut the budget deficit to the target of three percent of gross domestic product required by the Maastricht treaty to join EMU's starting line-up in 1999.
Waigel has also come under fire over a plan to revise up the value of the Bundesbank's gold reserves, a move he says would help cut both the national debt and the budget deficit.

Although Waigel cuts a powerful image on the international stage, his domestic influence is constrained since the forecasts on which he bases his budget are made by Rexrodt's department and unemployment outlooks come from the Labour Ministry.
"If (the Economics Minister) gets it wrong...then the Finance Minister has to cope with the consequences," Waigel told Spiegel in an interview from the magazine's Monday edition.
But, in a statement on official ministry paper, Rexrodt retorted: "It is always the Finance Ministry which presses for a more favourable economic forecast."

Unemployment, which peaked in January at a 64-year record of 4.7 million, has blown away Bonn's budget projections. And recent tax projections revealed a new gap of nearly 20 billion marks ($12 billion) in revenues this year.
Rexrodt's Free Democrat party (FDP), junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, passed a resolution on Sunday rejecting tax increases to plug the budget holes.
